newsitem.title: MEXICO: Arrested Mexican is not guerrilla chief, family says.
newsitem.headline: Arrested Mexican is not guerrilla chief, family says.

text.p: Mexico's government claimed it had arrested a leader of a feared Marxist guerrilla group but the suspect's family and a colleague said on Tuesday he was an innocent peasant activist.

Under the headline "EPR ringleader falls" the Interior Ministry announced in a statement on Monday evening that police had arrested alleged Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) rebel chief Benigno Guzman earlier in the day at his home in Mexico City.

Officials presented the arrest as a breakthrough in the government's war against the EPR, a violent rebel group that first appeared last June. The EPR has attacked mainly army and police posts, killing more than 30 people in a bid to force out President Ernesto Zedillo's government.
Local television showed images of Guzman wearing a green uniform and standing impassively behind bars on Tuesday in a jail in the tourist resort city of Acapulco.
But Guzman's wife, Sofia Bustamante, flatly denied that her husband was anything more than a peasant leader.

"He should be set free," Bustamante told Reuters in a telephone interview from her home -- where 20 armed police burst in on Monday and arrested Guzman as he was teaching his four young children to read.
"Benigno is innocent. He has done no harm to anyone," Bustamante said.

To back up its assertions, the family issued a statement entitled "The Interior Ministry Is Lying." It said Guzman was a founder of the OCSS, a peasant organisation in Guerrero, which had always worked within the law, and added:

"It has become a rule of the State during the present federal administration to arrest massively political opponents against whom criminal cases are fabricated and they are presented to public opinion as members of armed revolutionary organisations."
Some Mexican media were also cautious in reporting Guzman's arrest. "Benigno Guzman arrested; Interior Ministry calls him EPR ringleader," was the headline of the left-wing daily La Jornada.

A government spokesman said on Tuesday that other suspected EPR members had identified Guzman as a leader in confessions to the authorities. "We always had our doubts about an armed, radical wing existing within the civilian, activist organisation that was the OCSS," he said.
But Cecilia Corona, a leader of the FAC-MLN, a hard-left umbrella group for more than 400 grassroots organisations including the OCSS, attacked the government's version of events.
"It is totally unacceptable how the government, in an act of desperation, wants to show that in an election year it has solved the problem of the EPR," she told Reuters.

"Benigno is a decent man, a humble peasant who has fought to press the demands of his organisation and to denounce the repression he has suffered...the government is brutally repressing social organisations."

The FAC-MLN has complained that more than 200 left-wing activists up and down the country have been arrested as part of a national clampdown on suspected EPR members or sympathisers ahead of July congressional elections.
Opposition politicians also noted that Guzman had been arrested for crimes under state jurisdiction, whereas the offences of rebellion and terrorism are considered federal matters.
Asked about this, a government spokesman said Guzman's initial detention on murder, robbery and assault charges did not preclude the filing of other charges later.

Little is known about the EPR's structure or leaders, but leading commentator Raymundo Riva Palacio wrote in a column on Monday that the authorities feared the group might carry out a big kidnapping or assassination before the elections.
